topics.title: Chapter frame: four issues the chapter must cover

sourceRefs.evidence: This chapter addresses four issues: data communications, networks, the Internet, and protocols and standards.

concepts.title: Four chapter pillars
concepts.summary: Data communications, networks, the Internet, protocols and standards.

coverageRequirements.requirement: Open with the four-pillar roadmap so later sections are not orphaned facts.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Source explicitly structures the chapter around these four issues.

topics.title: Data communications: definition, effectiveness, five components

sourceRefs.evidence: Data communications are the exchange of data between two devices via some form of transmission medium.

concepts.title: Data
concepts.summary: Information presented in a form agreed by the parties creating and using it.

concepts.title: Telecommunication
concepts.summary: Communication at a distance (telephony, telegraphy, television).

concepts.title: Four effectiveness characteristics
concepts.summary: Delivery, accuracy, timeliness, jitter.

concepts.title: Jitter
concepts.summary: Variation in packet arrival time causing uneven audio/video quality.

sourceRefs.evidence: Jitter refers to the variation in the packet arrival time.

concepts.title: Real-time transmission
concepts.summary: Timely delivery of audio/video as produced, same order, without significant delay.

concepts.title: Five components of a data communications system
concepts.summary: Message, sender, receiver, transmission medium, protocol.

sourceRefs.evidence: A data communications system has five components.

relationships.note: Effectiveness of the system depends on how well the five components implement delivery/accuracy/timeliness/jitter.

definitions.definition: Exchange of data between two devices via some form of transmission medium such as a wire cable.
The information (data) to be communicated — text, numbers, pictures, audio, video.
The device that sends the data message (computer, workstation, telephone handset, video camera, …).
The device that receives the message.
Physical path by which a message travels from sender to receiver (twisted-pair, coaxial, fiber-optic, radio waves).
Set of rules that govern data communications; agreement between communicating devices. Without a protocol, connected devices may still not communicate.

inputs: some arrive with 30 ms delay, others 40 ms
examples.method: Compare arrival-time variation against production interval

coverageRequirements.requirement: Define delivery, accuracy, timeliness, and jitter with the source’s meaning — not only bandwidth.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Exam-relevant effectiveness criteria; absent from current chapter.

coverageRequirements.requirement: Keep all five components with the French/Japanese protocol analogy if space allows.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Core taxonomy of the section; review Q1 asks for the five components.

topics.title: Data representation: text, numbers, images, audio, video

sourceRefs.evidence: Information today comes in different forms such as text, numbers, images, audio, and video.

concepts.title: Bit pattern representation
concepts.summary: Text and numbers are represented as sequences of bits.

concepts.title: Unicode and ASCII
concepts.summary: Unicode (32-bit symbols in this source) covers world languages; ASCII is the first 127 characters / Basic Latin.

concepts.title: Code and coding
concepts.summary: A code is a set of bit patterns for text symbols; representing symbols is coding.

concepts.title: Images as pixel matrices
concepts.summary: Image = matrix of pixels; bit-pattern size depends on color depth; RGB mixes red/green/blue.

sourceRefs.evidence: Exercise 15 uses 16-bit color pixels.

concepts.title: Audio/video continuous vs discrete
concepts.summary: Audio is naturally continuous; video can be continuous (camera) or sequence of images. Both can be digital or analog.

relationships.note: ASCII characters are the first 127 of Unicode (Basic Latin) in this source.

definitions.definition: Coding system using 32 bits (per this source) to represent a symbol/character used in any language.
American Standard Code for Information Interchange; first 127 Unicode characters / Basic Latin.

formulas.name: Color count from pixel bit depth
formulas.meaning: Maximum distinct colors representable when each pixel uses a fixed bit pattern.
commonErrors: Confusing bits per pixel with total image memory

sourceRefs.evidence: Exercise 15: color image uses 16 bits per pixel; max colors = 2^16.

comparisons.title: Forms of information
comparisons.note: Text/numbers/images are bit patterns; audio/video may start continuous then become digital/analog.

coverageRequirements.requirement: Cover all five information forms; do not collapse to 'data' as a single blob.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Source gives distinct representation rules per form; review exercise 14–15 depend on it.

sourceRefs.evidence: Communication between two devices can be simplex, half-duplex, or full-duplex.

concepts.title: Simplex
concepts.summary: Unidirectional; one device transmits, the other only receives; entire channel capacity used one way.

concepts.title: Half-duplex
concepts.summary: Both can transmit and receive, but not at the same time; entire capacity taken by current transmitter.

concepts.title: Full-duplex (duplex)
concepts.summary: Both stations transmit and receive simultaneously; capacity shared via two paths or divided link.

relationships.note: Half-duplex can use full capacity per direction sequentially; full-duplex must share capacity continuously.

definitions.definition: Unidirectional communication (keyboard → monitor examples).
Two-way, one direction at a time (walkie-talkies, CB radios).
Simultaneous two-way communication (telephone network).

examples.title: Device examples per mode
examples.method: Map each device to directionality model

confusions.title: Half-duplex vs Full-duplex
confusions.trap: Both are 'two-way'; only full-duplex allows simultaneous send+receive.

sourceRefs.evidence: Review Q7 asks the difference.

coverageRequirements.requirement: All three flow modes with direction semantics and at least one device example each.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Current chapter table is thin and invents speed claims not in source.

sourceRefs.evidence: A network is a set of devices (often referred to as nodes) connected by communication links.

concepts.title: Network
concepts.summary: Set of devices (nodes) connected by communication links.

concepts.title: Node
concepts.summary: Computer, printer, or any device capable of sending and/or receiving data.

concepts.title: Distributed processing
concepts.summary: Task divided among multiple computers; each handles a subset instead of one large machine.

sourceRefs.evidence: Review Q2 asks advantages of distributed processing.

concepts.title: Network criteria
concepts.summary: Performance, reliability, security.

concepts.title: Performance metrics
concepts.summary: Transit time, response time; evaluated as throughput vs delay — often contradictory.

sourceRefs.evidence: If we try to send more data… we may increase throughput but we increase the delay.

concepts.title: Reliability
concepts.summary: Frequency of failure, recovery time, robustness in catastrophe.

concepts.title: Security
concepts.summary: Protect from unauthorized access/damage; policies for recovery from breaches.

relationships.note: Throughput and delay are often contradictory under congestion.

definitions.definition: A set of devices connected by communication links.
Networking performance metric of data successfully transferred (often desired higher).
Performance metric of time cost (often desired lower); increases with congestion.

confusions.title: Bandwidth vs throughput
confusions.left: bandwidth (not defined in this Ch.1 extract)
confusions.trap: Current Washi chapter invents a bandwidth-centric formula narrative; this source teaches throughput/delay tradeoff instead.

coverageRequirements.requirement: Teach performance, reliability, security as the three network criteria.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Review Q3; missing from current chapter.
Key relationship that summarization usually deletes.

sourceRefs.evidence: There are two possible types of connections: point-to-point and multipoint.

concepts.title: Link
concepts.summary: Communications pathway transferring data between devices.

concepts.title: Point-to-point connection
concepts.summary: Dedicated link between two devices; entire capacity reserved.

sourceRefs.evidence: IR remote example.

concepts.title: Multipoint (multidrop) connection
concepts.summary: More than two devices share a single link; capacity shared spatially or temporally.

concepts.title: Physical topology
concepts.summary: Geometric representation of relationship of links and nodes.

concepts.title: Mesh topology
concepts.summary: Every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device.

concepts.title: Star topology
concepts.summary: Each device has a dedicated link only to a central hub/controller.

concepts.title: Bus topology
concepts.summary: Multipoint; one long backbone cable; drop lines and taps.

concepts.title: Ring topology
concepts.summary: Each device connected to two neighbors; signal passed device-to-device; each device has a repeater.

concepts.title: Hybrid topology
concepts.summary: Combination, e.g. star backbone with bus branches.

relationships.note: Mesh is built from dedicated p2p links.
Bus is the multipoint topology example.
Hub is a single point of failure: hub down ⇒ whole system dead.

definitions.definition: Dedicated link between two devices; entire capacity reserved for those two.
Connection in which more than two specific devices share a single link.
Connection running between the device and the main bus cable.
Connector that splices into or punctures the cable sheathing to contact the metallic core.
Central controller in a star topology that exchanges frames between devices.

formulas.name: Fully connected mesh duplex links
formulas.meaning: Number of duplex-mode physical links in a fully connected mesh of n nodes.
commonErrors: Using n(n-1) without dividing by 2 when links are duplex

sourceRefs.evidence: we can say that in a mesh topology, we need n(n-1)/2 duplex-mode links.

formulas.name: Mesh I/O ports per device
formulas.meaning: Each mesh device needs n−1 I/O ports to reach the other n−1 stations.
commonErrors: Answering cable count when ports were asked

sourceRefs.evidence: every device on the network must have n - 1 I/O ports.

topics.title: Categories of networks: LAN, WAN, MAN

sourceRefs.evidence: A LAN normally covers an area less than 2 mi; a WAN can be worldwide.

concepts.title: LAN
concepts.summary: Privately owned; single office/building/campus; few km; resource sharing; often bus/ring/star.

concepts.title: WAN
concepts.summary: Long-distance over large geographic areas; switched WAN vs point-to-point WAN.

concepts.title: MAN
concepts.summary: Size between LAN and WAN; town/city; high-speed connectivity (DSL, cable TV).

concepts.title: Switched WAN
concepts.summary: Connects end systems via routers; examples X.25, Frame Relay, ATM.

concepts.title: Point-to-point WAN
concepts.summary: Leased line from telco/cable provider connecting home or small LAN to ISP.

relationships.note: Determined primarily by size; MAN sits between.

definitions.definition: Local area network: privately owned, links devices in a single office/building/campus; currently limited to a few kilometers.
Wide area network: long-distance transmission over large geographic areas (country/continent/world).
Metropolitan area network: size between LAN and WAN, covering a town or city.

examples.title: MAN via DSL or cable TV

comparisons.title: LAN vs MAN vs WAN
comparisons.note: Do not invent speed tables unless sourced; this chapter emphasizes size and examples.

sourceRefs.evidence: When two or more networks are connected, they become an internetwork, or internet.

concepts.title: Internetwork / internet
concepts.summary: Two or more connected networks.

concepts.title: Heterogeneous enterprise mix
concepts.summary: Two LANs (bus + star) plus president computer joined via switched WAN backbone and p2p WANs.

sourceRefs.evidence: Figure 1.12 heterogeneous network of four WANs and two LANs.

relationships.note: The Internet (uppercase) is the most notable internetwork.

definitions.definition: Two or more networks that can communicate with each other.

examples.title: East/west offices + president remote
examples.method: Lease backbone switched WAN; connect each site with p2p WAN
examples.result: Four WANs + two LANs heterogeneous internetwork

confusions.title: Network vs Internet
confusions.trap: Network = devices+links; Internet = huge collection of interconnected networks.

sourceRefs.evidence: Review Q11.

coverageRequirements.requirement: Keep the heterogeneous two-LAN + WAN scenario as the worked illustration.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Primary source example of internetworking; absent from current chapter.

topics.title: The Internet: history and ISP hierarchy

sourceRefs.evidence: An internet (note the lowercase letter i) is two or more networks that can communicate with each other.

concepts.title: The Internet
concepts.summary: Uppercase I; collaboration of hundreds of thousands of interconnected networks; structured system.

concepts.title: ARPANET history
concepts.summary: ARPA/DoD motivation; 1967 ACM proposal; 1969 four nodes (UCLA, UCSB, SRI, Utah); NCP; 1972–73 Cerf/Kahn; TCP split into TCP/IP.

concepts.title: TCP/IP split
concepts.summary: IP handles datagram routing; TCP handles segmentation, reassembly, error detection.

concepts.title: IMP
concepts.summary: Interface message processor: specialized computer connecting hosts; IMPs connect to each other.

concepts.title: ISP hierarchy
concepts.summary: International → national (backbone, NAPs, peering) → regional → local.

concepts.title: NAPs and peering points
concepts.summary: NAPs are third-party switching stations between national backbones; peering points are private interconnects (up to 600 Mbps in source).

relationships.note: NCP provided early host communication; later replaced by TCP/IP.
Today most end users connect via local ISPs; hierarchy is conceptual not geographic.

definitions.definition: Organization providing Internet connectivity; may be international, national, regional, or local.
Complex switching station (often third-party) connecting national backbone ISPs.

examples.title: First ARPANET nodes
examples.method: Connect via IMPs; NCP for host communication

comparisons.title: International vs National vs Regional vs Local ISPs

confusions.title: internet vs Internet
confusions.trap: Lowercase = any internetwork; uppercase = the global system.

coverageRequirements.requirement: Preserve 1960s–1973 timeline: ARPA, ARPANET, IMP, NCP, Cerf/Kahn, TCP/IP split.
coverageRequirements.rationale: High exam density; completely missing from current chapter.
Defines how the modern Internet is organized in this source.

sourceRefs.evidence: The key elements of a protocol are syntax, semantics, and timing.

concepts.title: Protocol key elements
concepts.summary: Syntax (structure/format), semantics (meaning of bit sections), timing (when/how fast).

concepts.title: Entity
concepts.summary: Anything capable of sending or receiving information.

concepts.title: Syntax
concepts.summary: Structure/format/order of data (e.g., first 8 bits sender address, next 8 receiver, rest message).

concepts.title: Semantics
concepts.summary: Meaning of each section of bits and the action to take.

concepts.title: Timing
concepts.summary: When data should be sent and how fast; sender 100 Mbps vs receiver 1 Mbps overloads receiver.

relationships.note: Syntax + semantics + timing together define a protocol.

definitions.definition: Set of rules governing data communication; defines what, how, and when to communicate.

examples.title: 100 Mbps sender vs 1 Mbps receiver
examples.method: Compare production rate to processing rate

coverageRequirements.requirement: Always teach syntax/semantics/timing together when defining protocol.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Review Q12; current chapter only has a thin one-line definition.

sourceRefs.evidence: Data communication standards fall into two categories: de facto and de jure.

concepts.title: Why standards are needed
concepts.summary: Ensure products from different manufacturers work together.

sourceRefs.evidence: Review Q13.

concepts.title: De facto standards
concepts.summary: Not approved by organized body; adopted through widespread use.

concepts.title: De jure standards
concepts.summary: Legislated by an officially recognized body.

concepts.title: Standards organizations
concepts.summary: ISO, ITU-T (ex-CCITT), ANSI, IEEE, EIA; forums; FCC regulatory agencies.

concepts.title: Forums
concepts.summary: Special-interest groups that evaluate/standardize faster than formal committees.

concepts.title: RFC and Internet standard process
concepts.summary: Internet draft (6-month lifetime) → RFC; maturity levels and requirement categories.

relationships.note: Specification begins as draft, may become RFC, then Internet standard.

definitions.definition: Standard established by widespread use rather than official approval.
Standard legislated by an officially recognized body.
Published specification in the Internet standards process; idea/concept precursor to an Internet standard.

confusions.title: Protocol vs Standard
confusions.trap: Protocol = rules for communication; standard = rules agreed/recognized so products interoperate.

coverageRequirements.requirement: De facto/de jure + major orgs + RFC process.
coverageRequirements.rationale: Entire second half of source chapter; missing from current Washi chapter.
